passage: The engagement hall in Aminabad smelled of marigolds and frying kachoris. Asif had barely reached the buffet when Phuppo caught his sleeve. "Your cousin is settled at twenty-three. You're twenty-one now, so when is your turn?" He laughed and said something about exams. Two tables later, an uncle asked the same thing, then tapped his watch as if it were a joke. By the time the cake was cut, Asif had heard the question five times. He stepped out to the balcony, where his cousin Kashish was scrolling her phone. "Counting?" she asked. "Five," he said. "They mean well, I know. Phuppo cried at my school results." He stared at the traffic below. "But it feels like someone started a timer on me and forgot to ask if I wanted one." Kashish passed him a kachori and said nothing, which helped.

qa.a: Asif had heard the question five times by the time the cake was cut.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he said it felt like someone had started a timer on him?
qa.a: He felt pressured and a little trapped, even though he knew his relatives cared; he mentions that Phuppo cried at his school results, so the love is real, but the repeated question made him uneasy.

qa.q: What small step could help Asif at the next gathering?
qa.a: He could prepare one calm, friendly line, such as "I'll tell you when there's news," and perhaps ask a trusted relative like Kashish to change the subject when the questions pile up.

"Anjali, beta, come sit. Your Mama has something to tell you."
Kishore Mama was already holding his phone out. "Very good family, Pune. The boy is an engineer. I'll send your photo tonight, no?"

I used to mute the family chat group only during exams. Last winter I muted it for good.
It started with my cousin's wedding card. Someone replied under it, "Next is Bidisha?" with three laughing faces. Then an aunt wrote, "Don't wait too long, beta, good boys go fast." Twenty people reacted with hearts. I was in the college library, reading the same line of my notes again and again.
My cousin Mridul texted me privately a minute later: "Ignore them. Want me to post a dog photo to change the topic?" He did, and it worked for about an hour.
Looking back, nobody in that group wished me harm. My aunt sends me soup when I'm sick. But being asked in front of everyone made my life feel like a countdown I hadn't agreed to.

Walking back, she said, "If either of us says no after a few meetings, can we promise the families won't take it as an insult?" I said yes. That promise made me want to meet her again.

Pre-marriage conversation session, community centre, Saturday.
Aadhya and Gautam came with both mothers for their second meeting. The families had already exchanged horoscopes and were keen. I asked each person to write three things they wanted in a home life, then read them aloud.
Aadhya wrote: time for her music, living near her parents for a few years, sharing chores. Gautam wrote: a quiet home, a dog, and room to change jobs. Both mothers laughed at the dog.
When I asked, "What would make you say no?" Gautam's mother began answering for him. Gautam touched her arm and answered himself: "If one of us felt we couldn't say no." Aadhya looked at him for a long moment and smiled.
Next step: I suggested two more meetings without the mothers, in a café, and asked both families to agree that either answer is acceptable. Both agreed.

qa.a: Gautam wrote: a quiet home, a dog, and room to change jobs.

qa.a: It suggests she felt relieved and reassured, because Gautam's answer showed he also wanted both of them to keep the freedom to say no.

qa.a: It gives Aadhya and Gautam space to speak for themselves, as Gautam had to when his mother began answering for him, and to decide freely.

Monday. Vinita's mother handed her a printout: Raghav, twenty-four, six feet, government job, same community. "Perfect on paper," her mother said. Vinita folded it into her notebook and felt nothing at all.
Two weeks later, a Sunday. Vinita and Raghav walked around the lake for three hours. She asked how his family argued. He said, "Loudly, then we eat together." She told him she hated loud rooms. He paused. "Then I'd need to learn to argue softer. Could you teach me?" She laughed, surprised.

Sit, Abhinav. You asked how I chose your grandfather, so I'll tell you properly.
I was a girl of twenty when the proposals started. My uncle brought a stack of horoscopes and photographs. One boy was a doctor, fair, tall; everyone was thrilled. I met him once. He talked for an hour about his car and never asked me a single question.
Your grandfather's proposal came later. Shorter, a clerk, and my aunt sniffed at that. But at our second meeting he asked what I was reading, and when I said poetry, he asked me to recite one. Then he listened, really listened.
I told my father, "I want more time with the clerk." Papa was surprised, but he allowed three more meetings. By the third, I knew.
Fifty years, Abhinav. Not once did he stop asking my opinion. That is what I, Aadhya, would look for again.

Told Divyansh everything today, on the terrace of his hostel. About Salma. About the eight months. About how I lie to Ma every Saturday and say I'm at the library.

I was twenty-five, working in the railway office. One evening your great-grandfather said, "The girl's family has agreed. The date is in April. You'll meet her at the engagement." That was all. My consent was a formality, a nod.
